/lgtm

/lgtm

> What CPU regulator punishes a process with excessive CPU utilization?

The problem is that any such limiter applies globally, punishing all requests. Network bandwidth throttling is particularly disruptive.

To summarize: the desire is to severely punish / throttle write requests which we know will trigger a large number of watch events. The watch events are sent in parallel to the extent possible, but the physical resources have limits (obviously). Both a width penalty and extra latency are therefore appropriate.

> all the requested work gets done, it just takes longer to get done

Right, this is how network bandwidth throttling works too. But it is still catastrophic, because it throttles important requests along with unimportant ones, and the throttling is so severe that nothing can complete before timeouts. (and then retries keep it in that condition.) It might actually be better if the process *were* killed, it may be more likely to recover in that case.

> I do not see how watch notifications can starve mutations. Eventually all the notifications will be sent and the mutations will resume, even if the golang scheduler is that hostile.

The problem is not the golang scheduler, the problem is network bandwidth. E.g. imagine 1000 nodes with 10 services each covering 1000 pods and you do a rolling restart. Every pod change results in a change to an Endpoints object; there are 10 such objects, and each change generates an event for a watcher on each of the 1000 nodes. That is O(nodes * services * pods) total work, 10,000,000 total notifications if there is no batching. A big endpoints object can be, say, 500kib. That is 5TiB of network traffic. (In practice, there is some batching, and even if not, the first few notifications slow everything down so much that there is effectively more batching-- if the system continues to work at all.)

I am not sure if the problem is that the network egress prevents any mutating requests from coming into apiserver, or if it just prevents apiserver from saying anything back, but it doesn't matter. If you trigger this condition, apiserver--in fact, everything on the VM it is on-- doesn't respond to most requests for a very long time.

EndpointSlices help but don't eliminate the problem. And users can create the problem in other ways with other resources if they try.

I think the best way to make sure we support the use case is to make an integration (or e2e if not possible) test that exercises the scenario. The test should be general and not depend on a particular fix implementation.

Then we should merge the stupidest thing that fixes that test without breaking other scenarios. This unlocks a large amount of value (e.g. we can start removing client side rate limits).

Then I think Mike's concerns come to the top. Optimizing stuff in the presence of good, general tests is fun and profitable :)

In that middle state, while this is (likely) excessively punitive, I think we'd want users to configure this so that such requests went to priority levels that were focused around the resource in question (e.g. endpoints).

>  what would an integration or e2e test that checks under-utilization look like?

The test I had in mind is to verify there's not OVER-utilization. And to do that I would set up the test scenario, e.g. X watchers of Y things updated as fast as possible, and verify that the number of watch events generated is below some threshold.

I am not worried about underutilization, I think that can be optimized later. If what we end up with is grossly underutilized, I believe we can change constant factors until it works in practice, and optimize for real later.

Yeah, update supports creating but you have to know the name.

Instead of making this a construction setting (which adds a lot of complexity and constrains all callers to doing the same thing), I would do this:

* Override the Add method (as you have done) and make it do what you called "promote" (I think you are right that the current behavior is surprising)
* Add an `AddOutOfBand` method and make it do what you called "ignore" (pass through to underlying queue)
* Add an `AddIfNotDelaying` method to support the last mode.

I think @deads2k should sign off on this

> we also need to be able to adjust the immediate add behaviour when an item is popped out of the waiting channel in the waitingLoop() (when the clock has advanced past the delay time)

Why would anyone want something other than the "promote" behavior for this? (I didn't read the entire diff)

In general we should *not* give people a choice like this without an extremely good reason.

> They way I have implemented it (with the constructor option) allows a client of the package to change the queue behaviour by changing a single line of code (the call to create the queue).

But my suggestion of changing the default fixes it for ~everyone just by recompiling! I think probably no one wants the current behavior?

> someone doing something funky like trying to use multiple of the different Add behaviour functions against the same delayed queue because it will be very easy to get surprising behaviour with unintended consequences

Sure, I'd be fine with actually not allowing the pass-through option at all (edit: maybe? I have to think more?). But in general I think the person making a call to Add is in the best position to decide what this should do to pending calls for the same thing if it's already in the queue.

I think it is better to think of the delaying/rate-limiting as a tool to help you hit a target, and not as a cop to guarantee you don't exceed the target. It clearly works that way today, and I think it's best to keep it that way.

I think it is reasonable for people calling Add to decide whether they're making sure the thing is the queue, or adding it now (removing it from the queue). We can document that only the former choice obeys the rate limit in all cases.

The current behavior of having duplicate calls is at least 90% bug IMO. Maybe @deads2k recalls some reason for it to work this way?
Just fyi this is in my queue but the code change is still more complicated than I expected so it might be a bit before I get to it.
OK, I read a bit more, I'm still hung up on people having to decide what behavior they want at construction time. Why shouldn't the caller of `Add` be able to decide what operation they want?

No worries! (and sorry if this is outdated, I think you wrote a few messages while I was writing this)

Correct me if I'm wrong -- we only keep one copy of something in the waiting queue, we don't use this for calendaring (scheduling multiple adds in advance). So:
* `AddAfter(,0)` should always act like promote, or something is wrong, no? It would be extremely surprising if AddAfter(,0) added a long delay, no matter how the queue behaved otherwise. The point of the heap is to be able to take the earliest value, right?
* `AddAfter` with a short enough duration should also essentially be promote, right?

I agree AddAfter with 0 should accomplish the same thing as AddAfter with a short non-zero delay.

The one that is confusing is just plain old Add. Today it always means "ignore the queue and do something out of band". If we make it mean "promote" then actually it'll mean "delete any queue item and do it now". If instead we make it mean "wait", it'll effectively mean "do it later if it's in the queue, now otherwise". I guess I think we should make Add mean promote, because that's most similar to today's behavior, and because it'll be predictable. We could add a "AddIfNotWaiting" method for the other behavior?
